1. Sources, prerequisites, notation and learning route

The core synthesis uses Oxford M1 Linear Algebra I (lecturer Andrew Wathen), MIT18.06SC (Gilbert Strang), Berkeley Math54 (Alexander Paulin), and ETH Zurich Linear Algebra for Computer Scientists PartII (Afonso S. Bandeira and Robert Weismantel). Stanford EE263, CMU21-241 and Harvard Math55a were compared as additional written sources. Exact documents, page ranges, selection reasons and corrections are in the source audit. Exercises are reconstructed with independent solutions; no complete copyrighted assignment collection is reproduced.

You need span, independence, rank–nullity, basis coordinates and matrix multiplication. Declare the field and inner product before computing. We mainly work in finite-dimensional real spaces. The complex extension uses conjugate linearity in the first argument and linearity in the second:

⟨x,y⟩G=x*Gy,x*=x¯T.

Here G is Hermitian positive definite; the standard case is G=I. On real spaces conjugations disappear. A generator matrix has generators as columns. An orthonormal column matrix Q∈Fm×r need not be square. We distinguish P (a projector), G (a metric), and R (an upper triangular factor). Animations distinguish exact algebraic checkpoints from illustrative movement. A planar drawing does not replace a proof in arbitrary dimension.

2. What an inner product adds to a vector space

Vector-space axioms alone define neither length nor perpendicularity. An inner product adds these through additivity, the declared scalar convention, conjugate symmetry and strict positivity:

⟨x,y⟩=⟨y,x⟩¯,⟨x,x⟩>0(x≠0).

The induced norm and distance are

‖x‖=⟨x,x⟩,d(x,y)=‖x−y‖.

The square root is essential: the self-product scales by |α|2, whereas length scales by |α|. Positivity means that a vector orthogonal to itself is zero. With the indefinite form G=diag(1,−1), the nonzero vector (1,1)T has self-product zero. Such a form is not an inner product; our norm and minimization proofs cannot be transferred to it.

For G=diag(1,4), vectors (1,1)T and (4,−1)T are perpendicular in the weighted metric, although their ordinary dot product is three. Orthogonality belongs to the chosen metric, not merely to the coordinate labels.

3. Gram matrices and positive definiteness

For a basis (b1,…,bn) define Gij=⟨bi,bj⟩. Expanding both arguments gives

⟨∑ixibi,∑jyjbj⟩=x*Gy.

A real inner product has a symmetric positive definite Gram matrix; a complex one has a Hermitian positive definite Gram matrix. Conversely such a matrix defines an inner product. Symmetry alone is insufficient: diag(1,0) gives zero length to a nonzero vector. In dimension two, completing the square gives

G=(abbc),xTGx=a(x1+bax2)2+(c−b2a)x22.

Thus G is positive definite exactly when a>0 and ac−b2>0. For any generator matrix A,

z*A*Az=‖Az‖2,ker(A*A)=kerA.

The kernel equality follows in both directions by multiplying or by strict positivity. Therefore rank(A*A)=rankA, and A*A is invertible exactly when the columns are independent.

4. Cauchy–Schwarz, equality and angles

For y≠0, subtract the component along y:

r=x−y⟨y,x⟩⟨y,y⟩.

The residual satisfies ⟨y,r⟩=0. Expansion yields

0≤‖r‖2=‖x‖2−|⟨y,x⟩|2‖y‖2.

Hence |⟨y,x⟩|≤‖y‖‖x‖, with equality precisely when r=0, meaning linear dependence. If y=0, the inequality is immediate and equality holds. In real space the unsigned angle between nonzero vectors is

θ=arccos!(⟨x,y⟩‖x‖‖y‖),0≤θ≤π.

Cauchy–Schwarz makes the arccosine input admissible. Orthogonality gives θ=π/2, never a negative unsigned angle. A zero vector has no defined angle. A complex product may be nonreal, so this real arccosine formula cannot be used unchanged.

5. Pythagoras, triangle inequality and polarization

For real vectors,

‖x+y‖2=‖x‖2+2⟨x,y⟩+‖y‖2.

Perpendicularity removes the middle term. Bounding it by 2‖x‖‖y‖ and taking nonnegative square roots proves the triangle inequality. Equality requires vectors in the same nonnegative direction, including zero; arbitrary dependence is insufficient because opposite vectors cancel.

In real space the Pythagorean equality also implies perpendicularity. In complex space it forces only Re⟨x,y⟩=0. The imaginary part can remain nonzero. Real products can be reconstructed from lengths:

⟨x,y⟩=‖x+y‖2−‖x−y‖24.

Consequently a real linear norm-preserving map preserves products. A translation preserves distances but need not preserve norms measured from the origin.

6. Orthogonal sets and coefficient extraction

A pairwise orthogonal list is independent if every vector is nonzero. Indeed, from ∑ciui=0 one gets

0=⟨uj,∑iciui⟩=cj‖uj‖2.

Strict positivity forces every coefficient to vanish. Dividing each nonzero vector by its norm produces an orthonormal list. For a vector in its span,

x=∑jcjuj,cj=⟨uj,x⟩‖uj‖2.

The denominator disappears only for unit vectors. Under the opposite complex convention, argument order must be changed consistently. For a nonorthogonal basis, coefficients are coupled by a Gram system rather than obtained by independent division.

For example, (3,−1)T and (1,3)T are perpendicular and have squared norm ten. The coefficients of (1,2)T are 1/10 and 7/10. Multiplying by the corresponding basis vectors reconstructs (1,2)T. These are coefficients in an unnormalized basis, not coefficients in its normalized version.

7. Orthogonal complements and a unique decomposition

Define

W⊥={x∈V:⟨w,x⟩=0 for every w∈W}.

Linearity in the second argument proves that this is a subspace. Testing a spanning list suffices because perpendicularity extends to every linear combination. Also W∩W⊥={0}, because a common vector is perpendicular to itself.

In finite dimension extend an orthonormal basis of W to one of V, then split each vector's expansion into the two basis groups. This proves

V=W⊕W⊥,dimW⊥=dimV−dimW,(W⊥)⊥=W.

Uniqueness follows from the zero intersection. A chosen algebraic complement need not be perpendicular. Empty intersections are impossible: every subspace contains zero. For arbitrary infinite-dimensional subspaces, the decomposition theorem needs additional completeness/closedness hypotheses and is not inferred from the finite proof.

8. Four fundamental subspaces and consistency

For A∈ℝm×n, row space and nullspace live in ℝn; column space and left nullspace live in ℝm. The equation Ax=0 tests perpendicularity to every row, so

Row(A)⊥=kerA,Col(A)⊥=kerAT.

Their dimensions are r,n−r,r,m−r, where r=rankA. Equal row and column ranks do not give equality of all four dimensions. In complex space use conjugate transpose and identify the row-side subspace with Col(A*).

The system Ax=b is consistent exactly when b is perpendicular to every vector in kerA*. A left-null vector with nonzero product against b certifies inconsistency. This explains why the least-squares residual belongs to the left nullspace.

9. Projection onto a line

For u≠0, seek p=cu whose residual is perpendicular to the line. The equation ⟨u,x−cu⟩=0 gives

p=u⟨u,x⟩⟨u,u⟩,r=x−p,⟨u,r⟩=0.

In Euclidean real coordinates, Pu=uuT/(uTu). Rescaling u by any nonzero scalar leaves the projector unchanged. A zero generator describes the zero subspace, whose projector is zero; the division formula itself is undefined.

With u=(2,1)T and x=(1,3)T, the coefficient is one, p=(2,1)T, r=(−1,2)T and the squared distance is five. The product uTr=0 is a separate check rather than a visual guess.

10. Projection onto a subspace and the closest-point proof

For an orthonormal basis q1,…,qr of W, set

PWx=∑j=1rqj⟨qj,x⟩.

The result belongs to W, and its residual is perpendicular to each basis vector. It therefore realizes the unique perpendicular decomposition, proving independence of the selected orthonormal basis.

For any w∈W,

‖x−w‖2=‖x−PWx‖2+‖PWx−w‖2.

The two difference vectors are perpendicular. The unique closest point is consequently PWx, and equality in the minimum occurs only for that point. The same proof establishes ‖PWx‖≤‖x‖, with equality precisely for x∈W.

11. Projector matrices and the oblique distinction

Let Q contain an orthonormal column basis. Then P=QQ* and

P2=P,P*=P,imP=W,kerP=W⊥.

All positive powers equal P. The complement I−P swaps image and kernel, and P(I−P)=0. A Euclidean real matrix is an orthogonal projector if and only if it is symmetric and idempotent. For the converse, idempotence splits x=Px+(I−P)x, while symmetry makes the terms perpendicular.

Idempotence alone gives an oblique projection. For

P=(1200),

the vertical unit vector maps to (2,0)T, increasing length. The kernel is span{(−2,1)T}, which is not perpendicular to the horizontal image. The geometric distinction changes norm and minimum-distance conclusions.

Idempotence does not imply perpendicularity

Compare the oblique residual direction with the vertical Euclidean normal; exact lengths show expansion.

Idempotence holds, but symmetry and Euclidean norm contraction fail.

12. General basis formula and dependent generators

For independent columns of A∈Fm×r, write p=Ac. Perpendicularity gives

A*(x−Ac)=0,c=(A*A)−1A*x,P=A(A*A)−1A*.

The inverse is valid by the Gram-kernel theorem. The final matrix is m by m. Dependent columns make the Gram matrix singular; choose a column basis B instead. This changes coefficient bookkeeping but leaves the physical subspace and projector unchanged.

Coefficients may be nonunique even though the projected vector is unique. For A=(u,2u), every pair satisfying c1+2c2=α gives p=αu. A pseudoinverse selects a particular coefficient representative; it is not needed to define the unique projection.

13. A complete plane projection with two checks

Let W be the plane normal to n=(1,1,−1)T. The vector (1,2,3)T already belongs to it. For y=(1,2,4)T, one has nTy=−1, hence

PWy=y−nTynTnn=(4/37/311/3).

First check: nTPWy=0. Second check: the residual is −n/3 and is normal to the plane. Its squared norm is 1/3. The independent matrix expression PW=I−nnT/3 gives the same result. These checks catch sign errors and confusion between arbitrary complements and perpendicular ones.

14. Bessel, Parseval and partial expansions

For an orthonormal list spanning W,

‖x‖2=∑j=1r|⟨qj,x⟩|2+‖x−PWx‖2.

Dropping the nonnegative residual proves Bessel's inequality, with equality exactly for x∈W. A basis of the entire space makes the residual always zero and gives Parseval's identity. A partial list therefore gives an inequality, not an automatic identity.

If ‖x‖2=14 and two orthonormal coefficients are two and minus one, the squared distance to their span is 14−4−1=9. The projected vector has squared norm five; the original vector need not have that norm.

15. Gram–Schmidt and its ordered-span invariant

For independent ordered inputs, set v1=a1 and recursively compute

vk=ak−∑j<kvj⟨vj,ak⟩‖vj‖2,qk=vk‖vk‖.

Assume earlier outputs are mutually perpendicular and span the same input prefixes. Taking the product with vi cancels exactly the i th projection term. A zero residual would place ak in the preceding input span, contradicting independence. The difference ak−vk lies in that span, so both enlarged prefixes agree. This completes the induction; normalization preserves both span and perpendicularity.

The result depends on input order and sign/phase choices, whereas the final subspace projector does not. A dependent list can be processed by skipping exact zero residuals; dividing by them is invalid. A floating-point zero test needs a scale-aware tolerance and is a numerical judgment.

Gram–Schmidt: subtracting every earlier component

Coordinate columns show exact three-dimensional states. Orthogonality is certified algebraically; no planar angle is claimed.

Each removal uses the exact product and squared length of an earlier perpendicular output.

16. A full three-column orthogonalization

Take a1=(1,1,0)T, a2=(1,0,1)T and a3=(0,1,1)T. The first squared norm is two. The second projection coefficient is 1/2, giving v2=(1/2,−1/2,1)T with squared norm 3/2. The third coefficients against v1 and v2 are 1/2 and 1/3, so

v3=(−2/3,2/3,2/3)T,‖v3‖2=4/3.

Normalize to obtain

q1=(1,1,0)T2,q2=(1,−1,2)T6,q3=(−1,1,1)T3.

Check all three cross-products and all three lengths. Unit lengths alone do not give orthonormality, and neither does independence alone.

17. Reduced QR, rectangular dimensions and uniqueness

Set Q=(q1,…,qr) and R=Q*A. Prefix-span preservation gives Rij=0 for i>j, and normalization gives Rjj=‖vj‖>0. Therefore

A=QR,Q*Q=Ir,Q∈Fm×r,R∈Fr×r.

This reduced QR does not make rectangular Q invertible. For uniqueness with positive real diagonal, suppose QR=Q~R~. The matrix U=Q*Q~=RR~−1 is unitary and upper triangular. Column orthogonality successively forces it to be diagonal; its positive diagonal entries must all be one. Both factors consequently agree. Without the sign condition, signs or complex phases can move between factors.

Dependent input produces a singular triangular factor. A rank-revealing decomposition then requires separate choices.

Reduced QR: exact column contributions

Q is four by three; the diagram shows its actual four-component vectors and triangular coefficient pattern.

All three physical contributions sum to the original input column. The zero pattern is triangular.

18. Least squares is projection plus coefficient recovery

Minimizing ‖b−Ac‖ finds the closest point in Col(A). Independent columns give a unique coefficient vector; dependent columns give a unique physical minimizer but potentially many coefficients. The residual always satisfies A*(b−Ac)=0.

For independent columns and A=QR, the normal equations simplify to

Rc=Q*b,‖b−Ac‖2=‖b‖2−‖Q*b‖2.

Use back substitution rather than an explicit inverse. The norm identity independently checks an exact examination calculation. In floating-point work forming A*A worsens conditioning; QR avoids that formation. Detailed numerical stability and SVD theory belong to later chapters.

19. Weighted projection

With ⟨x,y⟩G=x*Gy, residual perpendicularity is A*G(x−Ac)=0. Hence

PG=A(A*GA)−1A*G,PG2=PG,PG*G=GPG.

The projector need not be ordinarily symmetric. For G=diag(1,4) and line generator (1,1)T,

PG=15(1414).

Applied to (2,0)T it gives (2/5,2/5)T. The residual (8/5,−2/5)T has zero weighted product with the generator. Euclidean perpendicularity and Euclidean minimum distance do not follow; the minimization is in the weighted norm.

20. A skewed basis transports the metric

Under physical synthesis x=Sc, coefficient products use Gnew=S*GS. This is congruence, while an operator representation changes by similarity Pnew=S−1PS. Self-adjointness becomes

Pnew*Gnew=GnewPnew.

For S=(1101) and physical horizontal projection, the coefficient projector is (1100), while the Gram matrix is (1112). The representation remains orthogonal in the transported metric despite its ordinary nonsymmetry. A coordinate matrix cannot be classified geometrically without its basis metric.

21. Function products and polynomial parity

On continuous real functions on [a,b], a<b, define ⟨f,g⟩=∫abfg. A continuous nonzero function is bounded away from zero on a small interval, so its squared integral is positive. Arbitrary pointwise functions lack that property: changing one point leaves an integral unchanged. In L2, functions equal almost everywhere are identified.

On [−1,1], odd functions are perpendicular to even ones. In basis (1,t,t2) the Gram matrix is

G=(202/302/302/302/5).

Monomials are independent but not orthogonal. Orthogonalization gives 1,t,t2−1/3 with squared norms 2,2/3,8/45. The odd polynomial t3 projects to zero onto the even span of 1,t2: both numerator integrals vanish. Onto the different span of 1,t, its projection is (3/5)t and its squared error is 8/175. The choice of subspace is decisive.

Parity decides the even-space projection

A finite polynomial projection is determined by zero odd integrals. This is not an infinite Fourier-convergence illustration.

The first and last curves describe target and residual, not a nonzero projected polynomial.

22. Finite Fourier expansions and sampled products

On [−π,π], ‖1‖2=2π and ‖coskt‖2=‖sinkt‖2=π for positive integer k. Distinct positive frequencies are perpendicular. Negative cosine frequencies repeat positive ones, and the zero sine is not a nonzero basis vector.

A finite trigonometric projection uses a finite coefficient sum. No exchange of an infinite sum and integral is required. Infinite Fourier convergence needs additional hypotheses and does not follow from finite orthogonality.

A sampled product ∑jwjp(tj)q(tj) is positive definite on degree-at-most- d polynomials when there are at least d+1 distinct real nodes with strictly positive weights. A nonzero polynomial cannot vanish at that many distinct points. Too few distinct nodes permit a nonzero vanishing polynomial and produce a semidefinite form.

23. Orthogonal matrices and Householder reflection

A square real matrix is orthogonal if QTQ=I, so Q−1=QT. Complex unitary matrices use conjugate transpose. A rectangular orthonormal-column matrix is an isometric embedding but lacks a two-sided inverse.

For nonzero real v,

H=I−2vvTvTv

fixes v⊥ and sends v to −v. It is symmetric and satisfies H2=I, hence is orthogonal with determinant minus one. The complementary projector I−vvT/(vTv) has normal eigenvalue zero rather than minus one; it is not reflection.

To reflect x onto a different equal-length target y, take v=x−y. Equal squared lengths imply 2vTx=vTv, so Hx=x−v=y. For x=y the generator is zero; use identity rather than divide by zero.

Householder family with norm-preserving motion

The normal rotates from zero to forty-five degrees; every checkpoint and intermediate motion preserves output length.

Actual SVG rotations preserve vector length throughout in-flight movement. The endpoint operator remains a reflection.

24. Products, nested subspaces and alternating projections

Two orthogonal projectors have an orthogonal-projector product exactly when they commute. If PQ=QP, then (PQ)2=PQ and (PQ)*=PQ, with image equal to the intersection. Conversely symmetry of PQ implies PQ=QP.

For U⊆W, PUPW=PWPU=PU, and PW−PU projects onto W∩U⊥. For perpendicular subspaces, PUPW=0 and their projector sum gives projection onto the direct sum. General products and sums do not satisfy these conclusions.

For two real lines at angle θ, tr(PUPW)=cos2θ. Repeated alternating projection can converge toward the intersection while a single product is not its orthogonal projector. The bank derives the exact planar contraction rather than extrapolating a drawing.

Matrix spaces also have perpendicular decompositions. For real matrices use the Frobenius product ⟨X,Y⟩F=tr(XTY). Symmetric and skew-symmetric parts are perpendicular: pairing a diagonal term with a skew part gives zero, while off-diagonal terms cancel in pairs. Thus X=(X+XT)/2+(X−XT)/2 is an orthogonal splitting. Inside symmetric n -by- n matrices, trace is the product with I; the perpendicular projection onto trace-zero matrices is X−tr(X)I/n. One scalar normal direction is removed from dimension n(n+1)/2. This supplies the orthogonal interpretation of the authentic dimension revisit.

25. Implementation, numerical boundaries and a verification workflow

Hand calculations often stay simpler with unnormalized perpendicular vectors until the last step. The editable laboratory uses exact rational Gram systems and checks perpendicular residuals, projector identities and squared distances.

Modified Gram–Schmidt updates the current residual after each subtraction:

Q = empty list
for each input column a:
    v = a
    for each accepted unit column q:
        v = v - q * inner(q, v)
    if v has exact norm zero:
        record a dependency and continue
    append v / norm(v) to Q

Classical Gram–Schmidt computes the projection coefficients against the original current input column. In exact arithmetic both agree; rounding can make them differ. Reorthogonalization can help. Householder QR uses norm-preserving transformations. A stable algorithm does not make an ill-conditioned problem well-conditioned.

Verify the field, conjugations, metric, nonzero denominators, independence before inversion, dimensions and original basis. For projection the strongest economical checks are membership plus perpendicular residual. These verify the answer independently of how it was obtained.

26. Complete chapter summary

Positive definiteness provides length, perpendicularity and the independence of nonzero orthogonal vectors. In finite dimension every subspace has a unique perpendicular complement, and every vector splits uniquely into its subspace part and perpendicular residual.

Projection gives the unique closest point. Use QQ* for orthonormal columns, a Gram inverse for independent general columns, and a weighted Gram expression for a different metric. Idempotence alone may describe an oblique projector. Ordinary matrix symmetry depends on whether the basis is orthonormal.

Gram–Schmidt removes earlier components while preserving ordered spans. Its normalized output forms reduced QR, which turns full-column-rank least squares into triangular solution. Bessel measures omitted components; Parseval requires a complete expansion. Function and sampled-polynomial spaces obey the same finite-dimensional principles once their product conventions are specified.

Authentic examinations: explicit orthogonality revisits

Question 1. Explicit orthogonality revisit: Dimension of symmetric trace-zero matrices

Authentic examination · checked English adaptation

MSc CS 1405 · Q41 · PDF page 9. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

Let W be the vector space of real symmetric 4×4 matrices whose trace is zero. What is dimW?

1.
10
2.
9
3.
8
4.
7
Read the complete solution and reasoning

Correct option: 2.

A symmetric four-by-four matrix is determined by four diagonal entries and six entries strictly above the diagonal. Thus the full symmetric space has dimension ten. Trace is a nonzero linear functional on this space: for example, its value on E11 is one. Its kernel therefore has dimension 10−1=9, giving option 2. To see the independence directly, use the six matrices Eij+Eji for i<j and the three matrices E11−E44,E22−E44,E33−E44. Their distinct off-diagonal and first three diagonal coordinates prove independence, and the trace condition forces the remaining diagonal coordinate. Option 1 omits the independent trace constraint. Options 3 and 4 incorrectly subtract further constraints; symmetry has already been included in the count of ten. Under the Frobenius product, trace is the product with I. The trace-zero subspace is its perpendicular complement inside the ten-dimensional symmetric space. Thus exactly one nonzero normal direction is removed. The projector is X−tr(X)I/4, which is distinct from entrywise removal of the whole diagonal.

Question 2. Explicit orthogonality revisit: An orthonormal basis defines a projection, not a norm expansion

Authentic examination · checked English adaptation

PhD CS 1404 · Q31 · PDF page 8. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

Let {u1,…,un} be an orthonormal basis of a subspace U⊆ℝm, with n≤m. Define Px=∑k=1n⟨x,uk⟩uk. Which statement is false?

1.

P is idempotent.

2.

If x∈U, then Px∈U.

3.

For every x∈ℝm, ‖x‖2≤‖Px‖2.

4.

P is a linear operator from ℝm to U.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Correct option: 3.

Every image is a linear combination of the basis vectors, so it lies in U. Linearity follows from linearity of the real inner product in x. If x=∑akuk belongs to U, orthonormality gives ⟨x,uk⟩=ak, hence Px=x; in particular, P(Px)=Px. Moreover r=x−Px is orthogonal to every uk because ⟨r,uj⟩=⟨x,uj⟩−⟨x,uj⟩=0. The orthogonal decomposition gives ‖x‖22=‖Px‖22+‖r‖22, so the universally valid inequality is ‖Px‖2≤‖x‖2. The inequality in option 3 is not valid for arbitrary permitted subspaces: take U=span{(1,0)} and x=(0,1). Then Px=0 while ‖x‖2=1. If U=ℝm, both norms agree; that special case does not establish option 3 as a general statement. The animation uses a two-dimensional orthogonal decomposition with labelled actual lengths, rather than pretending to draw arbitrary m dimensions.

Original and reconstructed mathematical/conceptual problems

Question 1. A parameterized Gram form

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual synthesis

For G=(2tt3), find exactly which real t define an inner product. Explain both endpoints.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The form is symmetric. Completing the square gives 2(x1+tx2/2)2+(3−t2/2)x22. Strict positivity for every nonzero vector is therefore equivalent to 6−t2>0, or −6<t<6. At either endpoint the vector (−t/2,1)T is nonzero and has self-product zero, so the form is semidefinite, not an inner product. Outside the interval the same vector has negative self-product. Testing only the standard basis vectors would miss that obstruction.

Question 2. An indefinite counterexample

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual synthesis

For B(x,y)=x1y1−x2y2, determine whether u=(1,1)T is perpendicular to itself and whether this defines an inner product.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Compute B(u,u)=1−1=0 although u≠0. Thus it is an isotropic vector for this form. The form is symmetric and bilinear, but fails strict positivity; for example B((0,1),(0,1))=−1. Neither taking a square root as a real norm nor deducing independence from perpendicularity is valid. The intersection of a subspace and its perpendicular complement need not be the zero subspace under an indefinite form.

Question 3. Cauchy–Schwarz with all equality cases

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual synthesis

Prove |⟨x,y⟩|2≤‖x‖2‖y‖2 and characterize equality, including zero inputs.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

For y≠0, let r=x−y⟨y,x⟩/‖y‖2. Its product with y is zero and expansion gives ‖r‖2=‖x‖2−|⟨y,x⟩|2/‖y‖2≥0. Multiplying by the positive denominator proves the inequality. Equality means ‖r‖=0, hence x is a scalar multiple of y. If either input is zero, both sides vanish. Therefore equality is exactly linear dependence, interpreted to include zero vectors.

Question 4. Triangle equality is stronger than dependence

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual synthesis

Find the equality condition in ‖x+y‖≤‖x‖+‖y‖ for real vectors. Test x=(1,0)T, y=(−2,0)T.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Squaring shows that equality requires ⟨x,y⟩=‖x‖‖y‖. Cauchy–Schwarz gives dependence, and the positive sign requires the same nonnegative direction for nonzero inputs. Zero inputs also give equality. In the proposed test the left side is one and the right side is three, so equality fails despite dependence. The absolute-value equality in Cauchy–Schwarz must not be substituted for the signed equality needed here.

Question 5. A complex Pythagorean trap

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual synthesis

In ℂ, take x=1, y=i with ⟨x,y⟩=x¯y. Does ‖x+y‖2=‖x‖2+‖y‖2 imply perpendicularity?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The left side is |1+i|2=2, and the right side is also two. However ⟨x,y⟩=i≠0. Expanding a complex self-product introduces 2Re⟨x,y⟩, which vanishes here. Thus the real converse to Pythagoras cannot be transferred without controlling the imaginary part. Replacing the inner product by its real part changes the real vector-space structure and is a different interpretation.

Question 6. An orthogonal list containing zero

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual synthesis

Is the pairwise perpendicular list (0,e1,e2) independent? Give the corrected theorem.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

It is dependent because the coefficient one on the zero vector, with all other coefficients zero, is a nontrivial zero combination. Pairwise products still vanish. The corrected theorem requires all vectors in the orthogonal list to be nonzero. Then taking a product with each list vector isolates its coefficient times a strictly positive squared norm, forcing every coefficient to vanish.

If Qc=0, multiplying by QT gives c=QTQc=0. Hence the kernel is zero and the columns are independent, so necessarily r≤m. Rectangular Q does not have a two-sided inverse. Its transpose is a left inverse, and QQT is a projector onto its column space. This distinction is the point of the proof.

Question 29. Why the QR diagonal condition matters

Question 43. Sampled polynomial positivity

Find a Householder reflection sending x=(3,4)T to y=(5,0)T.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Both squared norms are25. Set v=x−y=(−2,4)T, whose squared norm is20 and product with x is ten. Thus Hx=x−2v(10/20)=x−v=y. Explicitly H=(3/54/54/5−3/5). It is symmetric, its columns are orthonormal, and its determinant is minus one. The construction works because target norms agree and x≠y.

Question 50. Noncommuting line projectors

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual synthesis

Let P=diag(1,0) and Q=12(1111). Is PQ an orthogonal projector?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The product is 12(1100). It is nonsymmetric, and squaring gives one half of that product rather than itself. Thus it is neither an orthogonal projector nor idempotent. Each factor separately is an orthogonal projector. Their image lines intersect only at zero, so projection onto their intersection is zero, not PQ.

Question 51. A product is a projector exactly under commutation

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual synthesis

Prove the necessary and sufficient commutation condition for the product of two orthogonal projectors to be an orthogonal projector.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

If they commute, (PQ)2=P2Q2=PQ and (PQ)*=QP=PQ. Its image belongs to both image spaces, and every common image vector is fixed by both, proving the intersection image. Conversely an orthogonal projector is self-adjoint, so PQ=(PQ)*=QP. This converse concerns orthogonal-projector products; ordinary idempotence alone is a different condition.

Question 52. Nested projectors subtract correctly

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual synthesis

For U⊆W, prove that PW−PU is an orthogonal projector and identify its image.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Nestedness gives PUPW=PU because projection onto W preserves all U components, and by transpose PWPU=PU. Thus (PW−PU)2=PW−PU and the difference is symmetric. Its outputs lie in W and have zero U component. It fixes every vector in W∩U⊥. Therefore that intersection is its image, with rank dimW−dimU.

Question 53. When a projector sum works

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual synthesis

For orthogonal projectors PU,PW, prove that their sum is an orthogonal projector if the subspaces are perpendicular.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Perpendicularity gives both products zero. The sum is symmetric, and its square is PU+PW, so it is an orthogonal projector. Its image is U⊕W. If the spaces coincide and are nonzero, the sum is 2PU, whose square is 4PU; therefore the general statement fails without the perpendicularity hypothesis.

Question 54. Alternating projections contract geometrically

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual synthesis

For P=diag(1,0) and Q=12(1111), find (PQ)k for k≥1.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Let M=PQ. Direct multiplication gives M2=M/2. Induction therefore gives Mk=2−(k−1)M=2−k(1100). It converges to zero, which is the projector onto the two image lines intersection. No finite positive power equals zero. This separates asymptotic alternating projection from an exact one-step intersection projector.

Question 55. Trace measures overlap of two lines

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual synthesis

For unit real vectors u,v, show tr(PuPv)=(uTv)2 and interpret its extremes.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Write Pu=uuT and Pv=vvT. Their product is u(uTv)vT, so its trace is (uTv)(vTu)=(uTv)2. This is cos2θ. Zero means perpendicular lines; one means the same line, including opposite generator orientations. A value strictly between zero and one indicates partial overlap without equality of subspaces.

Question 56. The adjoint in a weighted metric

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual synthesis

For T=(0100) and G=diag(1,4), compute the metric adjoint.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The identity ⟨Tx,y⟩G=⟨x,T†y⟩G gives TTG=GT†, hence T†=G−1TTG=(001/40). It differs from ordinary transpose. Substitution verifies xTTTGy=xTGT†y for every x,y. The Gram matrix must be invertible and positive definite under the inner-product interpretation.

Question 57. A constraint minimum has a normal component

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual synthesis

Find the real vector of minimum Euclidean norm satisfying x1+2x2=5.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The affine constraint has normal n=(1,2)T. Any feasible vector splits into a normal component plus a perpendicular component. The normal coefficient is forced to 5/(nTn)=1, so x0=(1,2)T. Every other feasible vector is x0+w with nTw=0, giving squared norm 5+‖w‖2. Thus x0 is the unique minimum. The proof uses a full perpendicular decomposition rather than guessing proportional coordinates.

Question 58. An orthonormal completion

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual synthesis

Complete q1=(1,1,1)T/3 and q2=(1,−1,0)T/2 to a real orthonormal basis.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

A normal vector to both satisfies x1−x2=0 and x1+x2+x3=0, so take (1,1,−2)T. Its squared length is six, giving q3=(1,1,−2)T/6. All products vanish and lengths equal one. The negative of q3 gives another valid completion; the subspace and projector do not determine orientation.

Question 59. Norm preservation requires linearity for products

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual synthesis

Explain why a real linear norm-preserving map preserves products, but a distance-preserving translation need not preserve norms.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Apply polarization to Tx,Ty and use linearity to replace Tx±Ty with T(x±y). Norm preservation then gives ⟨Tx,Ty⟩=⟨x,y⟩. A translation x↦x+a preserves differences and distances, but sends zero to a, whose norm is nonzero when a≠0. Thus it fails the norm condition and the linearity needed by the product argument.

Question 60. The zero and whole-space endpoints

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual synthesis

What are projection, complement and distance for W={0} and W=V?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

For the zero subspace, PW=0, W⊥=V and the distance is ‖x‖. For the whole space, PW=I, W⊥={0} and the distance is zero. These endpoints obey the same decomposition and norm rules. The zero-subspace case has an empty basis sum, not a zero-vector denominator in the line formula.

28. Final examination rules and difficult-case checks

Every rule is a complete statement with its admissibility conditions. The bank supplies the proofs and counterexamples behind them.

Final examination rules

Rule 1

Declare the field and inner product before using perpendicularity. A weighted Gram product can make ordinarily nonperpendicular vectors perpendicular.

Rule 2

A real Gram matrix defines an inner product exactly when it is symmetric positive definite. Symmetry and nonnegative diagonal entries alone do not suffice.

Rule 3

A complex Gram matrix must be Hermitian positive definite. Ordinary transpose cannot replace conjugate transpose.

Rule 4

In this chapter the first argument is conjugate linear and the second is linear. A source using the other convention requires translated coefficients.

Rule 5

Length is the square root of the self-product. Squared length scales by |α|2, while length scales by |α|.

Rule 6

Strict positivity is the reason a vector perpendicular to itself must be zero. The conclusion fails for indefinite bilinear forms.

Rule 7

For a symmetric matrix (abbc), positive definiteness is equivalent to a>0 and ac−b2>0.

Rule 8

A Gram matrix A*A is positive semidefinite for every matrix A, and positive definite exactly for independent columns.

Rule 9

The identity ker(A*A)=kerA holds over real and complex Euclidean spaces. Its proof uses ‖Ax‖2, not cancellation of a potentially singular factor.

Rule 10

Consequently rank(A*A)=rankA. The ambient dimension of the Gram matrix remains the number of columns.

Rule 11

Cauchy–Schwarz equality holds exactly for linearly dependent input vectors, including cases involving zero.

Rule 12

A real unsigned angle is defined only for nonzero vectors and lies in [0,π]. A negative right angle is not part of that convention.

Rule 13

A negative real product corresponds to an obtuse angle. A complex product does not generally define the same arccosine expression.

Rule 14

For real vectors, Pythagorean equality is equivalent to perpendicularity. For complex vectors it only forces the real part of the product to vanish.

Rule 15

Equality in the real triangle inequality requires the same nonnegative direction, or a zero input. Opposite dependent vectors do not generally give equality.

Rule 16

Polarization reconstructs real products from norms. A linear norm-preserving map therefore preserves real products.

Rule 17

A translation preserves distances but generally changes norms from the origin. Distance preservation does not by itself establish linearity.

Rule 18

Pairwise orthogonality gives independence only when every listed vector is nonzero.

Rule 19

Normalize a nonzero orthogonal vector by its own norm. A zero residual cannot be normalized.

Rule 20

Coefficients in an orthogonal basis are ⟨uj,x⟩/‖uj‖2 under the chapter convention. Unit-length denominators disappear only after normalization.

Rule 21

In an orthonormal complex basis the analysis coefficient is ⟨qj,x⟩. Reversing the arguments conjugates it.

Rule 22

A nonorthogonal basis couples coefficients through its Gram matrix. Independent scalar projection coefficients cannot replace that system.

Rule 23

The Gram matrix in an orthogonal but unnormalized basis is diagonal with the basis squared norms. Summing coefficient squares without those weights is wrong.

Rule 24

Testing a spanning list suffices to characterize its perpendicular complement. Testing only one generator of a larger span does not.

Rule 25

Every perpendicular complement is a subspace. The intersection with the original subspace contains zero and, for an inner product, contains no other vector.

Rule 26

In finite dimension dimW+dimW⊥=dimV. The dimension refers to the same stated ambient space.

Rule 27

In finite dimension (W⊥)⊥=W. Infinite-dimensional versions can require closure and completeness hypotheses.

Rule 28

An algebraic complement need not be perpendicular. A direct-sum decomposition alone does not prove a minimum-distance property.

Rule 29

Row space and nullspace belong to the domain coordinate space. Column space and left nullspace belong to the codomain coordinate space.

Rule 30

For a real m -by- n matrix of rank r, the four dimensions are r,n−r,r,m−r. They are not generally all equal.

Rule 31

The row-side perpendicular complement is kerA, and the column-side perpendicular complement is kerA*. In complex coordinates the row-side space is identified through conjugation.

Rule 32

A system Ax=b is consistent exactly when every left-null vector is perpendicular to b.

Rule 33

One left-null vector with nonzero product against b is a certificate of inconsistency.

Rule 34

Perpendicular complements reverse inclusions: if U⊆W, then W⊥⊆U⊥.

Rule 35

The identity (U+W)⊥=U⊥∩W⊥ follows directly from the definition.

Rule 36

In finite dimension (U∩W)⊥=U⊥+W⊥. Do not silently transfer the statement to unrestricted infinite-dimensional subspaces.

Rule 37

A nonzero line generator gives Pu=uu*/(u*u). Nonzero scalar rescaling does not alter this projector.

Rule 38

A zero generator defines the zero subspace, whose projector is zero. The line division formula itself remains undefined.

Rule 39

A projected vector is certified by membership in the target subspace and a perpendicular residual. Either condition alone is insufficient.

Rule 40

A perpendicular residual belongs to the perpendicular complement; it is a vector and is not equal to that entire subspace.

Rule 41

Projection onto an orthonormal column basis is QQ*, with physical dimension equal to the ambient space.

Rule 42

For rectangular orthonormal Q, Q*Q=I but QQ* generally is a proper projector. A two-sided inverse is available only in the square case.

Rule 43

The perpendicular projector is independent of which orthonormal basis spans its subspace.

Rule 44

The closest-point proof compares squared distance with a sum of two nonnegative squared lengths. Equality identifies a unique minimizer.

Rule 45

Perpendicular projection contracts the norm: ‖Px‖≤‖x‖. Equality holds exactly for vectors already in the target subspace.

Rule 46

A Euclidean projector is orthogonal exactly when it is self-adjoint and idempotent. Neither property alone is enough.

Rule 47

Every idempotent splits its space into image plus kernel, even when the splitting is oblique.

Rule 48

An oblique projector can increase Euclidean length and need not produce the Euclidean closest point.

Rule 49

For an idempotent, all positive powers equal the matrix and trace equals rank. Symmetry is unnecessary for those algebraic facts.

Rule 50

The complementary projector is I−P. Its image and kernel are the original kernel and image.

Rule 51

A full-column-rank basis gives P=A(A*A)−1A*. Invertibility of the Gram matrix is a hypothesis, not an automatic property of generators.

Rule 52

For dependent generators, select an independent column basis or use an appropriate pseudoinverse. Never invert their singular Gram matrix.

Rule 53

A physical projection remains unique even when generator coefficient representations are not unique.

Rule 54

For a hyperplane through zero with real normal n≠0, subtract n(nTx)/(nTn). The distance is |nTx|/‖n‖.

Rule 55

Projection onto a shifted affine plane includes a constant term. It need not be a linear operator.

Rule 56

Bessel uses an orthonormal list and leaves a nonnegative residual term. Equality means membership in that list's span.

Rule 57

Parseval holds for a complete orthonormal expansion. A partial list does not automatically give norm equality.

Rule 58

Squared distance to an orthonormal span is the original squared norm minus the sum of captured coefficient magnitudes squared.

Rule 59

Gram–Schmidt preserves every ordered input prefix span, not merely the final span.

Rule 60

At each orthogonalization step remove all preceding accepted components. Removing only the immediately previous vector is generally insufficient.

Rule 61

Independent inputs produce nonzero exact Gram–Schmidt residuals. A zero residual diagnoses membership in the preceding span.

Rule 62

A dependent column can be skipped while later columns are still processed. Permanent termination can miss later independent directions.

Rule 63

Changing input order generally changes orthonormal outputs and intermediate spans. The final projector is unchanged if the final span is unchanged.

Rule 64

Unnormalized orthogonalization often preserves rational arithmetic. Normalize only when an orthonormal output or QR factor is required.

Rule 65

Reduced QR for an m -by- r full-column-rank matrix has Q of size m by r and R of size r by r.

Rule 66

The reduced QR factor R=Q*A is upper triangular because later orthonormal vectors are perpendicular to earlier input prefixes.

Rule 67

With standard Gram–Schmidt normalization, R has strictly positive real diagonal. This fixes sign or phase ambiguity.

Rule 68

Without the diagonal convention, valid QR factors can change column signs or phases while preserving their product.

Rule 69

Gram–Schmidt on an invertible real upper triangular matrix produces signed standard coordinate vectors. Positive input diagonal gives the unsigned canonical basis.

Rule 70

For independent columns, least squares reduces to Rc=Q*b and triangular back substitution.

Rule 71

For dependent columns, a least-squares fitted physical vector is unique but its coefficients may form an affine family.

Rule 72

The least-squares residual lies in kerA*. Its norm can be checked using perpendicular decomposition without reconstructing every coefficient.

Rule 73

In weighted geometry use A*GA and A*Gb. The resulting projection minimizes the weighted norm, not an unstated Euclidean norm.

Rule 74

Weighted perpendicular projection obeys P*G=GP and P2=P. Its coordinate matrix can be ordinarily nonsymmetric.

Rule 75

A basis change transports the metric by congruence S*GS, while an operator matrix changes by similarity S−1PS.

Rule 76

Integral products are strictly positive on continuous nonzero functions on a nondegenerate interval. Arbitrary pointwise function spaces require care about almost-everywhere equivalence.

Rule 77

On a symmetric interval odd functions are perpendicular to even functions. This can eliminate all coefficients before doing lengthy integrals.

Rule 78

Sampled products on degree-at-most- d polynomials need at least d+1 distinct nodes with positive weights for strict positivity.

Rule 79

Trigonometric cosine indices with opposite signs duplicate the same function. Distinct absolute frequencies, not merely distinct integers, determine distinct cosine directions.

Rule 80

The constant Fourier function has a different squared normalization from nonzero sine/cosine frequencies. The zero sine cannot be normalized into a basis vector.

Rule 81

Householder reflection fixes a perpendicular hyperplane and reverses its normal. Projection deletes the normal instead; the two operators are different.

Rule 82

A product of two orthogonal projectors is an orthogonal projector exactly when the factors commute. Its image is then their image-space intersection.

Rule 83

Nested projector differences and perpendicular-space projector sums have valid projection interpretations. General sums and differences require separate checks.

Rule 84

Exact algebra, a numerical tolerance and an illustrative animation serve different purposes. Use exact membership, residual, metric and identity checks to certify an examination answer.

29. Editable exact projection laboratory

Use two through four rows and one through four generator columns. Separate matrix rows with semicolons and entries with commas. Target entries are integers from minus ten through ten. Provide one positive integer weight from one through ten for each row; all ones give Euclidean geometry. Dependent and zero generators are accepted by retaining an independent column basis. Invalid input preserves the previous valid result. Every walkthrough starts paused.
